title: Howard Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Howard wells have a 105 ft median depth, 8 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $12,800-$22,500.
h1: What Wells Are Like Around Howard, Colorado
intro_html:
Buying land around Howard means dealing mainly with mountain bedrock, not a predictable basin aquifer. Records within 5 miles show a median well depth of 105 feet and a median reported yield of 8.0 gallons per minute. Those figures are useful for planning, but they are not a guarantee for a particular lot.

Most permits are for domestic or household use, and 1,223 wells identify unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers. Neighboring well locations, construction records, water rights, septic setbacks, and access for a drilling rig all deserve review before you commit to a property.

sections.heading: Howard Well Depths Depend on Fractured Mountain Bedrock
sections.html:
The 1,251 permitted wells in the Howard area have a median reported depth of 105 feet. The middle half runs from 63 to 215 feet, so a driller's bid based on the median alone can be misleading. About 43% are under 100 feet, while 42% fall between 100 and 300 feet.

Deeper holes are part of the local picture: 13% are between 300 and 600 feet, 2% are deeper than 600 feet, and the deepest record is 1,100 feet. Granite and gneiss can carry water in fractures rather than in a uniform layer. A nearby well is useful evidence, but it does not eliminate the risk of drilling farther or finding a different fracture pattern.

sections.heading: Expected Well Yield Near Howard
sections.html:
Among the 495 records reporting pump yield, the median is 8.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is 5.0 to 12.8 gallons per minute. That is a workable range for many household systems, but the reported number is a well test result, not a promise that the same flow will continue indefinitely.

Yield distribution is generally favorable in these records: 62% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute, 19% report more than 15 gallons per minute, and 19% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute. No reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute. Ask for the original pump test, recovery information, pump setting, storage capacity, and any seasonal limitations before treating a yield figure as dependable household supply.

sections.heading: Howard Water Levels and the Recorded Trend
sections.html:
Only 70 wells report a static water level, so the water-level sample is much smaller than the depth or permit sample. In those records, the median depth to water is 55 feet, with the middle half from 42 to 125 feet below the surface. That helps with pump planning, but the water level on a specific parcel can vary sharply in fractured rock.

The decade figures do not show a simple decline in this dataset. The median measured level was 76 feet below surface in the 2010s and 54 feet in the 2020s, meaning the later sample was shallower. Because the number of measurements is limited and the wells may differ, do not use this comparison alone to predict long-term water availability.

sections.heading: Who Has Drilled Around Howard, and When
sections.html:
Howard has a long permit history. Records begin with 1 permit in the 1950s, rise to 171 in the 1970s and 182 in the 1980s, then reach 303 in the 1990s. There are 181 permits from the 2000s, 119 from the 2010s, and 66 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The most common names in the records are American Drilling Service with Dewberry, Bradford W., at 378 wells; American Drilling Service Inc. with Dewberry, Noble, at 195; and Ma-Bel Drilling with Lively, Mabel, at 54. These records show who worked locally, not who is available today. Confirm licensing, insurance, references, and current pricing before choosing a driller.

sections.heading: What a New Howard Well May Cost
sections.html:
Local ground conditions are fractured mountain bedrock, described in the cost model as granite and gneiss. The drilling rate is estimated at $65 to $100 per foot. At the 105-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $6,800 to $10,500.

A finished system is more than the borehole. The estimate for a completed well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is $12,800 to $22,500 at that median depth. A deeper hole, difficult access, additional casing or grout, long utility runs, and changes in site layout can move the actual bid higher. Get the drilling price, casing, pump, testing, and allowances separated in writing.

sections.heading: Howard Risks to Check Before You Build
sections.html:
Low yield is not the only concern. Fractured-bedrock wells can produce water at one location and miss a useful fracture nearby, creating the possibility of a dry hole or a need to deepen the well. Review neighboring permits and construction reports near Coaldale, Cotopaxi, and other nearby areas, while recognizing that geology can change across a short distance.

The mapped environmental record includes 213 historic mine features within about 10 miles, with no PFAS sampling or contamination sites and no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. A mine feature is a reason to investigate location and water quality, not proof that a well is contaminated. Test the water after construction and again when appropriate. Confirm septic setbacks, well access, building envelopes, and the permit's allowed use before finalizing plans.

sections.heading: Buying or Building on a Howard Lot
sections.html:
Before closing, obtain the DWR permit, construction report, pump test, water-quality results, and maintenance history for the existing well. Of the 1,251 permits in the area, 834 are recorded as constructed, 905 report total depth, and 495 report pump yield. Missing records do not automatically mean a problem, but they make field verification more important.

For a vacant lot, have a driller review access, rig setup, expected depth, casing and grout requirements, and the likely pump and electrical layout. Most local permits are domestic or household use, at 93% of the use mix. Confirm the permitted use and any augmentation requirements with Colorado DWR before adding irrigation, livestock, or other demands. Nearby Coaldale, Cotopaxi, and Salida can provide context, but the parcel's own records should control your decision.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Howard, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Howard is 105 feet. The middle half runs from 63 to 215 feet. About 43% are under 100 feet and 42% are between 100 and 300 feet, but some wells are much deeper, including a recorded depth of 1,100 feet. Fractured granite and gneiss make the neighboring well comparison important.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Howard, Colorado?
faq.a: The local drilling estimate is $65 to $100 per foot. At the 105-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $6,800 to $10,500. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $12,800 to $22,500. Access, depth, casing, grout, utility distance, and site conditions can change the final bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Howard?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 8.0 gallons per minute, based on 495 records. The middle half is 5.0 to 12.8 gallons per minute. About 62% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute, while 19% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute. A pump test and recovery information are more useful for evaluating an individual existing well.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Howard, Colorado?
faq.a: Permit records do not establish that a particular well is safe to drink. There are no mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites and no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles, but 213 historic mine features are mapped. Test the well for appropriate contaminants after construction and review the result with a qualified water professional.

faq.q: Should I inspect a well before buying land near Howard?
faq.a: Yes. Ask for the DWR permit, construction report, depth, pump yield, static water level, water-quality tests, and maintenance records. The area has 1,251 permitted wells, but only 495 report pump yield and 70 report static water level. For vacant land, have a driller assess access and likely bedrock conditions before relying on a budget or building schedule.
